headline: Land, learning and the work of growing food
summary: Black farmworkers, farmers, scientists and extension educators faced different barriers. These records follow land, wages, organizing, education and cooperative institutions—and show where gains were restricted or reversed.
coverageNote: Thirteen selected episodes, from the 1865 land allocation and reversal to the 2022 agroecology center. A farmer, hired farmworker and agricultural scientist do not share one hiring route. Institutional histories, legislation, participant accounts and archival catalogs answer different questions; none alone establishes a reader’s employment history.
question: Which land, employment, training or program record connects this history to the farm or institution where you work?

events.title: Black leaders seek land to make freedom economically possible
events.people: Garrison Frazier, Ulysses L. Houston and other Savannah Black church leaders; freed families
events.decisionMaker: General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15; President Andrew Johnson’s later restoration policy reversed much of the allocation.
events.barrier: Emancipation did not itself provide the land or capital needed to farm independently.
events.change: After meeting Black leaders in Savannah, Sherman reserved coastal land for freed families in plots of up to 40 acres.
events.outcome: Freedpeople occupied allotted land, but Johnson’s pardons and the Freedmen’s Bureau’s September 1865 circular returned much of it to former owners.
events.limit: This was a geographically limited wartime order, not a national grant of permanent ownership. A family’s particular allotment and subsequent title require local records.

source.locator: Sherman’s Special Order No. 15; January 16, 1865 manuscript and exhibit description
source.supports: The consultation, coastal allocation and military/congressional limits.

events.title: Federal funding reaches Black agricultural colleges through a segregated system
events.people: Black agricultural students and educators; Senator Justin S. Morrill
events.decisionMaker: Congress enacted the Second Morrill Act; state governments divided the funding between institutions.
events.barrier: Black students were excluded from many existing land-grant colleges.
events.change: The 1890 law required states receiving funds to admit without racial distinction or designate separate colleges for Black students.
events.outcome: A surviving 1892–93 federal table records the division of agricultural funds between Black and white institutions.
events.limit: The provision supported Black colleges while permitting segregation. A funding table does not establish equal resources, an individual admission or a graduate’s employment.

source.title: U.S. Capitol Visitor Center / National Archives · Division of agricultural funds, 1892–93
source.locator: African American Land-Grant Colleges; artifact description and funding table
source.supports: The admission condition and state division of agricultural-college funding.

events.title: George Washington Carver becomes Tuskegee’s director of agriculture
events.decisionMaker: Tuskegee Institute appointed Carver to direct agriculture; this account does not identify the formal appointing document.
events.barrier: An agricultural degree and access to an academic research appointment were separate stages of entry.
events.change: After agricultural degrees at Iowa State in 1894 and 1896, Carver joined Tuskegee’s staff.
events.outcome: The National Park Service dates his appointment as director of agriculture to October 8, 1896.
events.limit: This establishes Carver’s education and appointment at Tuskegee. It does not establish a hiring pathway for farmworkers or for another institution’s scientists.

source.title: National Park Service · George Washington Carver at Tuskegee
source.locator: Biography paragraph covering the 1894 and 1896 degrees and October 8, 1896 appointment
source.supports: Carver’s degrees and dated appointment at Tuskegee.

events.title: Thomas Campbell takes Tuskegee’s agricultural teaching to farmers
events.people: Thomas Monroe Campbell, George Washington Carver and Booker T. Washington
events.decisionMaker: Washington and Carver developed the traveling school; Tuskegee assigned alumnus Campbell to operate it.
events.barrier: Many rural farmers could not travel to Tuskegee’s campus for instruction.
events.change: The Jesup Agricultural Wagon carried tools, seeds and demonstrations into farming communities.
events.outcome: Campbell’s extension assignment connected a Black agricultural educator’s work to farmers in Macon County, Alabama.
events.limit: This documents an educational service and a named assignment. It does not identify every participant or measure the program’s effect on each farm’s income.

source.title: Smithsonian NMAAHC · Tuskegee Institute’s Movable Schools
source.locator: Tuskegee Institute’s Movable Schools; From the Jesup Wagon to the School on Wheels
source.supports: Campbell’s assignment and the movable school’s teaching work.

events.title: Elaine sharecroppers organize; survivors contest mob-dominated trials
events.people: Black sharecroppers, Frank Moore and fellow defendants; attorney Scipio Africanus Jones
events.decisionMaker: Local authorities prosecuted Black defendants after the violence; the U.S. Supreme Court required federal examination of their due-process claims.
events.barrier: Debt tied Black sharecroppers to landowners. Organizing in Phillips County, Arkansas, was met by racial violence in 1919.
events.change: The defendants and their lawyers challenged convictions reached under threats and intimidation. In Moore v. Dempsey (1923), the Court rejected dismissal of their federal challenge.
events.outcome: The expected federal hearing never occurred. The governor commuted the sentences in 1923 and granted indefinite furloughs in January 1925.
events.limit: This documented a route to challenge those convictions, not a farm-labor contract, recovered wages or protection against all later violence.

source.title: Federal Judicial Center · Moore v. Dempsey
source.locator: The Case; The Supreme Court’s Ruling; Aftermath and Legacy; 1923 opinion excerpts
source.type: Federal judicial history and primary opinion excerpts
source.supports: The sharecropping context, court ruling and subsequent release process.

sources.title: Arkansas State University · Southern Tenant Farmers Museum historical timeline
sources.supports: Jones’s defense and fundraising work for the Elaine defendants.

events.title: Amelia Boynton links agricultural education with land and civic independence
events.people: Amelia Boynton Robinson and Samuel William Boynton
events.decisionMaker: USDA employed Amelia as a home demonstration agent; the Boyntons organized teaching and registration efforts with rural communities.
events.barrier: Black rural families faced limited resources and Jim Crow barriers to voting and economic independence.
events.change: Amelia began home-demonstration work in Selma in 1929, teaching canning, nutrition and agricultural improvements.
events.outcome: She and Samuel taught farming and home economics while encouraging land purchase and voter registration; they later joined the Dallas County Voters League.
events.limit: The biography documents their work and aims, but does not provide an appointment letter, participant list or measured farm-income gains. This is not a claim that every extension position followed the same route.

source.title: National Park Service · Amelia Boynton Robinson
source.locator: Paragraphs on the 1929 USDA job, Samuel Boynton and rural teaching in the 1930s
source.supports: Her home-demonstration employment and the Boyntons’ combined teaching and organizing.

events.title: Sharecroppers build an interracial union; John Handcox helps organize it
events.people: Black and white tenant farmers and farmworkers; John Handcox, H. L. Mitchell and Henry Clay East
events.decisionMaker: An interracial group formed the Southern Tenant Farmers’ Union in Arkansas; workers organized locals and collective action.
events.barrier: Agricultural subsidy arrangements favored landowners while tenants and laborers faced eviction and low pay.
events.change: The union began in 1934. Handcox, a Black sharecropper, used songs, travel and organizing to bring workers together.
events.outcome: The university museum reports that the 1935 cotton-pickers’ strike increased pay per pound. Violence and persecution persisted; Handcox fled Arkansas in 1937.
events.limit: Sources establish organizing and a reported wage gain, not a payroll audit for every plantation. Founding-day accounts differ, so this entry uses the year.

source.locator: Historical/Biographical Note; founding, subsidy arrangements and persecution
source.supports: The union’s founding and labor context; the underlying collection was not inspected.

events.title: Federal minimum-wage protection reaches some agricultural workers
events.people: Black farmworkers and other hired agricultural workers
events.decisionMaker: Congress amended the Fair Labor Standards Act; the federal Wage and Hour Division administers its protections.
events.barrier: Agricultural labor had not shared the same federal wage protections as many other kinds of work.
events.change: Public Law 89-601 narrowed the agricultural exemption and set a phased minimum wage for covered agricultural employees, starting at $1 an hour.
events.outcome: The expansion reached some farmworkers but retained exclusions and an agricultural overtime exemption.
events.limit: This was an occupation-wide change, not a race-specific award. Coverage and actual payment at a named farm need separate evidence; the historical rate is not today’s wage guidance.

source.title: U.S. Statutes at Large · Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1966
source.supports: The narrowed exemption, retained overtime exclusion and agricultural wage schedule.

sources.title: U.S. Department of Labor · Agricultural employment under the FLSA
sources.locator: Fact Sheet 12, January 2025; Coverage and Requirements
sources.supports: Why an agricultural job title alone does not establish minimum-wage or overtime coverage.

events.title: Black farmers build a federation for cooperative business and land retention
events.people: Black farmers and representatives of 22 founding cooperatives
events.decisionMaker: Member organizations formed the Federation of Southern Cooperatives; it later merged with the Emergency Land Fund.
events.barrier: Small Black farmers needed collective business support and help retaining their land.
events.change: Founded in 1967, the Federation linked cooperative development with advocacy. The 1985 merger expanded its land-protection services.
events.outcome: Its institutional record documents assistance with jointly owned businesses, farm enterprises and land retention.
events.limit: The organization’s history establishes its services and institutional changes. It is not an independent measure of acres saved, wages earned or benefits received by a particular member farm.

source.title: Federation of Southern Cooperatives/Land Assistance Fund · History
source.supports: The founding, merger and stated land-retention work.

sources.locator: Opening description of 22 founding cooperatives; services and cooperative principles
sources.supports: The founding membership and forms of cooperative support.

events.title: Fannie Lou Hamer organizes land and food through Freedom Farm
events.people: Fannie Lou Hamer and Freedom Farm Cooperative members
events.decisionMaker: Hamer founded the cooperative using a donation from Measure for Measure; members cultivated the land.
events.barrier: Poor Black farmers and sharecroppers depended on landowners for access to land and livelihood.
events.change: In 1969 Hamer purchased 40 acres in Mississippi’s Delta for collective cultivation.
events.outcome: The cooperative grew cash crops for expenses and vegetables for participating workers, later expanding its land and adding a pig bank.
events.limit: The cooperative failed in 1976, according to the archival biography. This is a local shared-land and food-security record, not proof of a permanent wage job or a connection to another farm.

events.title: Shirley and Charles Sherrod help build New Communities on collectively held land
events.people: Shirley Sherrod, Charles Sherrod, Slater King and New Communities participants
events.decisionMaker: Movement participants formed New Communities; its board arranged a financed land purchase in Lee County, Georgia.
events.barrier: Sharecroppers and tenants could lose homes and work when they participated in civil-rights organizing.
events.change: New Communities used collective landholding to seek a more secure economic base. It closed on 5,735 acres in January 1970.
events.outcome: The farm raised crops and livestock, but debt, drought and discriminatory lending contributed to the loss of its original land to foreclosure.
events.limit: The corporation survived the land loss. Founding a land trust did not guarantee secure livelihoods for all participants; it is not evidence about another farm’s employment.

source.title: SNCC Digital Gateway · New Communities formed in Southwest Georgia

source.supports: The founders, land purchase, farming activity and loss of the original land.

events.title: Black farmers obtain a claims process for USDA discrimination
events.people: Black farmer plaintiffs in Pigford v. Glickman
events.decisionMaker: U.S. District Judge Paul L. Friedman approved the parties’ consent decree on April 14, 1999.
events.barrier: Farmers challenged discriminatory denial and delay of USDA loans and benefits and failures to resolve their complaints.
events.change: The settlement established procedures for deciding claims and reviewing errors.
events.outcome: GAO reported that by January 2006 about 14,300 claims had been approved for payments and benefits exceeding $900 million; about 8,100 had been denied.
events.limit: These are historical claims outcomes, not current eligibility guidance. The settlement did not compensate every farmer or prove access to any particular farm job.

source.title: U.S. GAO · Pigford Settlement: The Role of the Court-Appointed Monitor
source.locator: GAO-06-469R, March 17, 2006; opening settlement chronology and January 2006 claims totals
source.supports: The consent decree and claims outcomes reported by January 2006.

events.title: FAMU and Black food organizers open an agroecology center
events.people: Lola Hampton and Frank Pinder, the center’s namesakes; co-directors Kwasi Densu and Jennifer Taylor
events.decisionMaker: Florida A&M University and the National Black Food & Justice Alliance partnered to establish the center.
events.barrier: The partners identified a need for research and training shaped by Black farmers and underserved land stewards.
events.change: They created the Lola Hampton-Frank Pinder Center for Agroecology at FAMU.
events.outcome: Local reporting documented the November opening at the Orange Avenue garden, with classroom, laboratory and community-garden uses.
events.limit: The opening and named leadership are documented. The sources do not establish participant completion, paid placements or a particular reader’s employment.

source.title: National Black Food & Justice Alliance · FAMU agroecology center launch
source.locator: October 20, 2022 release; partnership, research aims and November launch plans
source.supports: The partners’ announced center, research aims and planned launch.

furtherResearch: Inspect local wage sheets, crew rosters and contracts to identify the employer and any wage change for a particular farmworker.
Trace a farm’s land through allotment, deed, lease and foreclosure records; distinguish the landowner from the operating business and labor contractor.
Read archival membership and activity records before connecting a farm or person to Freedom Farm, New Communities or the Federation.
Compare extension agents’ appointment, payroll and county reports with participant records; an educational program is not proof of paid placement.
Add local cases from more regions and periods. These episodes do not cover every Black farming community or every form of agricultural work.

credential.credential: Agricultural degrees at Iowa State College, 1894 and 1896
credential.record: The National Park Service records Carver’s Bachelor of Agriculture in 1894 and Master of Science in Agriculture in 1896.
credential.work: He became Tuskegee Institute’s director of agriculture in October 1896. His academic appointment is distinct from a farmworker hiring route.
